claim: Malaria causes hundreds of millions of infections and more than 600,000 deaths each year.
source: Malaria is an ancient and deadly scourge of humanity, with hundreds of millions of people infected by Plasmodium malaria parasites and more than 600,000 deaths each year (WHO, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2014 report

claim: Artemisinin-tolerant parasites have been identified in southeast Asia.
source: Recent identification of artemisinin-tolerant parasites in southeast Asia, however, has raised concerns that the broad potency of ACTs against all parasite strains may be waning, which could lead to a resurgence in malaria deaths (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ariey et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dondorp et al., 2009 and Ariey et al., 2014

claim: Heme is a ubiquitous biological cofactor required by nearly all organisms to carry out diverse redox biochemistry.
source: Heme is a ubiquitous biological cofactor required by nearly all organisms to carry out diverse redox biochemistry (Ponka, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ponka, 1999

claim: Plasmodium parasites sequester and biomineralize heme released during hemoglobin digestion in their acidic food vacuole.
source: Parasites sequester and biomineralize the copious heme released during large-scale hemoglobin digestion in their acidic food vacuole (van Dooren et al., 2012; Sigala and Goldberg, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to van Dooren et al., 2012 and Sigala and Goldberg, 2014

claim: Plasmodium parasites require heme as a metabolic cofactor for cytochrome-mediated electron transfer within mitochondria.
source: they also require heme as a metabolic cofactor for cytochrome-mediated electron transfer within mitochondria (Painter et al., 2007; van Dooren et al., 2012; Sigala and Goldberg, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Painter et al., 2007; van Dooren et al., 2012; and Sigala and Goldberg, 2014

claim: Plasmodium falciparum parasites encode and express all of the conserved enzymes for a complete heme biosynthesis pathway.
source: Sequencing of the Plasmodium falciparum genome over a decade ago and subsequent studies have revealed that parasites encode and express all of the conserved enzymes for a complete heme biosynthesis pathway (Figure 1A), but the role and properties of this pathway have been the subject of considerable confusion and uncertainty (Gardner et al., 2002; van Dooren et al., 2012; Sigala and Goldberg, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2002; van Dooren et al., 2012; Sigala and Goldberg, 2014, and reference to Figure 1A

claim: De novo heme synthesis is not required by intraerythrocytic parasites.
source: Recent studies, however, have clarified that de novo heme synthesis is not required by intraerythrocytic parasites and therefore is unlikely to be a viable target for therapeutic inhibition (Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagaraj et al., 2013 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: The parasite-encoded ferrochelatase can be knocked out to ablate heme biosynthesis but parasite growth is unaffected.
source: The parasite-encoded ferrochelatase (FC) can be knocked out to ablate heme biosynthesis but parasite growth is unaffected, suggesting that parasites can scavenge host heme to satisfy metabolic requirements during blood-stage infection.
evidence: Supported by inference from prior studies

claim: Parasites can scavenge host heme to satisfy metabolic requirements during blood-stage infection.
source: The parasite-encoded ferrochelatase (FC) can be knocked out to ablate heme biosynthesis but parasite growth is unaffected, suggesting that parasites can scavenge host heme to satisfy metabolic requirements during blood-stage infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FC knockout does not affect parasite growth

claim: Exogenous ALA stimulates PPIX production in P. falciparum parasites.
source: Prior work indicated that exogenous ALA stimulates PPIX production in P. falciparum parasites (Smith and Kain, 2004; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith and Kain, 2004 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: Parasites grown in 200 µM ALA display bright red fluorescence distributed throughout the infected erythrocyte.
source: Parasites grown in 200 µM ALA, however, display bright red fluorescence distributed throughout the infected erythrocyte, as expected for accumulation of PPIX (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: PPIX generates cytotoxic reactive oxygen species when photo-illuminated.
source: PPIX is also known to generate cytotoxic reactive oxygen species when photo-illuminated, owing to formation of an excited triplet state that can undergo collisional energy transfer with ground state triplet oxygen to produce highly reactive singlet oxygen (Celli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Celli et al., 2010

claim: Hemozoin motion in untreated parasites is unaffected by exposure to light that overlaps the excitation wavelength of PPIX.
source: Hemozoin motion in untreated parasites was unaffected by exposure to light that overlaps the excitation wavelength of PPIX (Videos 1, 2).
evidence: Supported by video data in Videos 1 and 2

claim: Hemozoin dynamics in ALA-treated parasites are rapidly ablated by light.
source: In contrast, the hemozoin dynamics in ALA-treated parasites were rapidly ablated by light (Videos 3, 4).
evidence: Supported by video data in Videos 3 and 4

claim: ALA-treated and illuminated parasites show loss of electron density within the digestive vacuole.
source: Ultra-structural analysis by electron microscopy revealed a loss of electron density within the digestive vacuole of ALA-treated and illuminated parasites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting disruption of the food vacuole membrane and outward diffusion of the vacuolar protein contents.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The growth of ALA-treated parasite cultures is strongly attenuated by light.
source: Whereas untreated parasite cultures grew normally in the presence of light, the growth of ALA-treated cultures was strongly attenuated by light (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with a prior report (Smith and Kain, 2004).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citation to Smith and Kain, 2004

claim: Succinylacetone fully rescues the photosensitivity of parasite growth in ALA.
source: The photosensitivity of parasite growth in ALA was fully rescued by 50 µM succinylacetone (SA), an ALA dehydratase (ALAD) inhibitor shown in previous work to substantially reduce PPIX biosynthesis from ALA in parasite-infected erythrocytes (Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Nagaraj et al., 2013 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: Parasite photosensitivity in ALA requires biosynthetic conversion of ALA to PPIX.
source: This chemical rescue confirmed that parasite photosensitivity in ALA requires biosynthetic conversion of ALA to PPIX.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SA blocks photosensitivity

claim: The parasite PBGD gene was successfully disrupted using single-crossover homologous recombination.
source: We successfully disrupted the parasite genes encoding the apicoplast-targed PBGD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the cytosolic CPO (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) using single-crossover homologous recombination to truncate the open reading frame for each gene.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The parasite CPO gene was successfully disrupted using single-crossover homologous recombination.
source: We successfully disrupted the parasite genes encoding the apicoplast-targed PBGD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the cytosolic CPO (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) using single-crossover homologous recombination to truncate the open reading frame for each gene.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Disruption of parasite PBGD and CPO genes had no effect on the ability of parasite-infected erythrocytes to incorporate 13C-labelled ALA into heme, PPIX, or coproporphyrinogen III.
source: Contrary to simple predictions, however, these genetic disruptions had no effect on the ability of parasite-infected erythrocytes to incorporate 13C-labelled ALA into heme, PPIX, or coproporphyrinogen III (CPP) (Figure 2A), as monitored by a previously developed LC-MS/MS assay (Ke et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2A and citation to Ke et al., 2014

claim: Clonal growth of ΔPBGD and ΔCPO parasite lines remained fully photosensitive in ALA.
source: and clonal growth of both parasite lines remained fully photosensitive in ALA (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: Parasites treated with doxycycline and IPP lack the intact apicoplast organelle.
source: The lethal effects of doxycycline, however, can be chemically rescued by IPP, which enables parasites to make essential isoprenoids despite apicoplast disruption. This rescue leads to a stable metabolic state in which parasites lack the intact organelle such that nuclear-encoded proteins ordinarily targeted to the apicoplast become stranded in small vesicles (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011

claim: Apicoplast loss in doxycycline and IPP-treated parasites was confirmed by disrupted apicoplast targeting of the nuclear-encoded ALAD enzyme.
source: We confirmed apicoplast loss in doxycycline and IPP-treated parasites by using microscopy to verify disrupted apicoplast targeting of the nuclear-encoded ALAD enzyme (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Apicoplast loss in doxycycline and IPP-treated parasites was confirmed by PCR showing loss of the small apicoplast genome.
source: PCR to confirm loss of the small apicoplast genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Supported by PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: Apicoplast loss in doxycycline and IPP-treated parasites was confirmed by western blot showing disruption of post-translational processing of ALAD.
source: and western blot (WB) to visualize disruption of post-translational processing of ALAD (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7

claim: Parasites with disrupted apicoplast retain their capacity for heme biosynthesis from ALA.
source: Despite apicoplast disruption, these parasites retained their capacity for heme biosynthesis (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2A

claim: Parasites with disrupted apicoplast remain fully photosensitive in ALA.
source: and remained fully photosensitive in ALA (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 2E

claim: Mature erythrocytes retain the cytosolic heme biosynthesis enzymes ALAD, PBGD, UROS, and UROD.
source: Proteomic studies have confirmed that mature erythrocytes retain the cytosolic enzymes (ALAD, PBGD, uroporphyrinogen synthase [UROS], and uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase [UROD]) (Pasini et al., 2006; D'alessandro et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pasini et al., 2006 and D'alessandro et al., 2010

claim: The vestigial heme biosynthesis pathway in erythrocytes is ordinarily quiescent due to the lack of ALA synthesis or uptake.
source: but this vestigial pathway is ordinarily quiescent due to the lack of ALA synthesis or uptake in erythrocytes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about erythrocyte metabolism

claim: Red porphyrin fluorescence in ALA-treated infected erythrocytes is detectable throughout the erythrocyte cytoplasm.
source: In support of this model, we noted that red porphyrin fluorescence in ALA-treated infected erythrocytes was not limited to the parasite but was detectable throughout the erythrocyte cytoplasm (Figure 1B), as expected for host enzyme activity and production of PPIX in this compartment.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B

claim: Filtered lysate supernatants from uninfected erythrocytes can synthesize 13C-labelled PPIX and CPP from 5-[13C4]-ALA.
source: We detected formation of 13C-labelled PPIX and CPP but not heme, and this biosynthetic activity was fully blocked by SA (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 3A

claim: Filtered lysate supernatants from uninfected erythrocytes cannot synthesize heme from 5-[13C4]-ALA.
source: We detected formation of 13C-labelled PPIX and CPP but not heme, and this biosynthetic activity was fully blocked by SA (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 3A

claim: Erythrocytes retain a vestigial and partial biosynthesis pathway capable of converting exogenous ALA into PPIX but are unable to convert PPIX to heme due to lack of mitochondria and FC.
source: These observations provide direct support for our model that erythrocytes retain a vestigial and partial biosynthesis pathway capable of converting exogenous ALA into PPIX but are unable to convert PPIX to heme due to lack of mitochondria and FC.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PPIX but not heme synthesis in erythrocyte lysates

claim: Uninfected erythrocytes show no detectable porphyrin fluorescence in the presence of ALA.
source: In contrast to parasite-infected erythrocytes, uninfected erythrocytes showed no detectable porphyrin fluorescence in the presence of ALA (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3B

claim: Electroporation of uninfected erythrocytes in the presence of ALA results in robust intracellular porphyrin fluorescence.
source: Electroporation of uninfected erythrocytes in the presence of ALA, however, resulted in robust intracellular porphyrin fluorescence (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3B

claim: The erythrocyte membrane has a low permeability to amino acids.
source: consistent with reports that the erythrocyte membrane has a low permeability to amino acids (Ginsburg et al., 1985; Kirk et al., 1994; Desai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ginsburg et al., 1985; Kirk et al., 1994; and Desai et al., 2000

claim: Plasmodium parasites export hundreds of effector proteins into host erythrocytes that establish new permeability pathways.
source: Upon invasion, Plasmodium parasites export hundreds of effector proteins into host erythrocytes. These proteins dramatically alter the architecture of the infected erythrocyte and establish new permeability pathways (NPPs) that enhance host cell uptake of amino acids and other nutrients from host serum (Spillman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spillman et al., 2015

claim: Parasites with normal protein export and permeability display robust PPIX fluorescence in ALA.
source: Whereas TMP-treated parasites with normal protein export and permeability displayed robust PPIX fluorescence indistinguishable from that of wild-type parasites, parasites incubated without TMP showed no detectable PPIX fluorescence (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3C

claim: Parasites with blocked protein export and permeability show no detectable PPIX fluorescence in ALA.
source: Whereas TMP-treated parasites with normal protein export and permeability displayed robust PPIX fluorescence indistinguishable from that of wild-type parasites, parasites incubated without TMP showed no detectable PPIX fluorescence (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3C

claim: Furosemide blocks parasite-derived NPP mechanisms directly.
source: We observed similar results in wild-type parasites using the small-molecule drug furosemide, which blocks parasite-derived NPP mechanisms directly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Staines et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Staines et al., 2004

claim: ALA is selectively taken up by infected erythrocytes via parasite-dependent nutrient-acquisition pathways and metabolized to PPIX by vestigial host enzymes within the erythrocyte cytoplasm.
source: We conclude that ALA is selectively taken up by infected erythrocytes via parasite-dependent nutrient-acquisition pathways and metabolized to PPIX by vestigial host enzymes within the erythrocyte cytoplasm (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and summarized in Figure 4

claim: Saponin-released asexual parasites fail to synthesize heme, PPIX, or CPP from 13C-ALA.
source: We failed to detect biosynthesis of heme, PPIX, or CPP in fractionated asexual and sexual blood-stage parasites (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 5D

claim: Saponin-released sexual gametocytes fail to synthesize heme, PPIX, or CPP from 13C-ALA.
source: We failed to detect biosynthesis of heme, PPIX, or CPP in fractionated asexual and sexual blood-stage parasites (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 5D

claim: The apicoplast-localized portion of the parasite heme biosynthesis pathway is largely or completely inactive during blood-stage infection.
source: suggesting that the apicoplast-localized portion of the parasite heme biosynthesis pathway is largely or completely inactive during blood-stage infection.
evidence: Inferred from the failure to detect heme biosynthesis in saponin-released parasites

claim: Parasites expressing apicoplast-targeted cobA-GFP show no red fluorescence in the apicoplast when treated with ALA.
source: We targeted a cobA-green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion protein to the apicoplast in ALA-treated parasites (Figure 6C) but were unable to detect any red fluorescence in this organelle indicative of cobA-mediated conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to the fluorescent products.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 6C, 6D, and 6E

claim: Parasite enzymes targeted to the apicoplast are inactive in both asexual and sexual blood stages.
source: This result suggests that parasite enzymes targeted to this organelle are inactive in both asexual and sexual blood stages (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of red fluorescence in cobA-expressing parasites treated with ALA, supported by data in Figure 6D and 6E

claim: Growth of ΔFC parasites is insensitive to light in the absence of ALA.
source: We also noted that growth of ∆FC parasites (Ke et al., 2014), which would be expected to accumulate PPIX during native pathway activity (Figure 1A), was insensitive to light in the absence of ALA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Ke et al., 2014

claim: Heme biosynthesis in blood-stage P. falciparum parasites is only operative when exogenous ALA is present to stimulate PPIX production by remnant host enzymes in the erythrocyte cytoplasm, with subsequent PPIX uptake and conversion to heme by FC in the parasite mitochondrion.
source: These observations suggest that heme biosynthesis in blood-stage P. falciparum parasites is only operative when exogenous ALA is present to stimulate PPIX production by remnant host enzymes in the erythrocyte cytoplasm, with subsequent PPIX uptake and conversion to heme by FC in the parasite mitochondrion (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations and summarized in Figure 4

claim: Luminol-based chemiluminescence can be used to photoactivate PPIX cytotoxicity in ALA-stimulated cells.
source: To bypass the need for external light, chemiluminescence has been proposed as an alternative means to photoactivate the cytotoxicity of PPIX in ALA-stimulated cells. Trial studies in cancer cell lines have shown modest success using the small molecule luminol (Laptev et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2012), whose iron-activated chemiluminescence (Rose and Waite, 2001) overlaps the absorbance spectrum of PPIX (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laptev et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2012; Rose and Waite, 2001, and data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The combination of ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol potently inhibits parasite growth.
source: The combination of all three compounds, however, potently inhibited parasite growth (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 7B

claim: Combination treatment with ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol causes widespread parasite death.
source: and microscopic examination by blood smear revealed widespread parasite death (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: Dd2 parasites with multidrug resistance remain susceptible to combination treatment with ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol.
source: In both parasite lines, combination treatment with ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol potently ablated parasite growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4

claim: Kelch-13 mutant parasites with artemisinin tolerance remain susceptible to combination treatment with ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol.
source: In both parasite lines, combination treatment with ALA, luminol, and 4-iodophenol potently ablated parasite growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4

claim: Artemisinin potently stimulates luminol chemiluminescence in vitro.
source: Artemisinin, whose endoperoxide moiety is reductively cleaved by intracellular iron to generate reactive oxygen radicals (Meshnick, 2002), has been shown to potently stimulate luminol chemiluminescence in vitro (Green et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to Meshnick, 2002 and Green et al., 1995

claim: The combination of ALA, luminol, and sub-therapeutic doses of dihydroartemisinin potently ablates parasite growth.
source: Single and double combinations had little effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 6), but all three compounds together potently ablated parasite growth, and growth inhibition could be fully rescued with SA (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 6

claim: The growth inhibition effects of ALA, luminol, and DHA combination can be fully rescued by SA.
source: but all three compounds together potently ablated parasite growth, and growth inhibition could be fully rescued with SA (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 7C

claim: Four of the eight heme biosynthesis pathway enzymes have been successfully disrupted in parasites.
source: Our work and recent studies have now successfully disrupted four of the eight pathway enzymes, providing firm evidence that de novo heme synthesis is dispensable during blood-stage infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study and prior studies

claim: Parasites have mechanisms to scavenge host heme to meet metabolic needs during blood-stage infection.
source: These data strongly suggest that parasites have mechanisms to scavenge host heme to meet metabolic needs and clarify that heme biosynthesis is not a viable target for classical drug inhibition (Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heme biosynthesis is dispensable, supported by citations to Nagaraj et al., 2013 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: Heme biosynthesis is not a viable target for classical drug inhibition in blood-stage parasites.
source: These data strongly suggest that parasites have mechanisms to scavenge host heme to meet metabolic needs and clarify that heme biosynthesis is not a viable target for classical drug inhibition (Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the dispensability of heme biosynthesis, supported by citations to Nagaraj et al., 2013 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: The parasite heme synthesis pathway is required for development within the mosquito and human liver.
source: Indeed, prior studies suggest that the parasite heme synthesis pathway is required for development within the mosquito and human liver (Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagaraj et al., 2013 and Ke et al., 2014

claim: Human serum contains 0.1–0.2 µM ALA.
source: Analytical studies have reported that human serum contains 0.1–0.2 µM ALA (Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011

claim: The 0.2 µM ALA natively present in human serum may be sufficient to stimulate low-level heme biosynthesis within parasites in vivo.
source: Thus, the 0.2 µM ALA natively present in human serum may be sufficient to stimulate low-level heme biosynthesis within parasites in vivo.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental observations

claim: Parasites grown in 1 µM 5-[13C4]-ALA produce detectable 13C-labeled PPIX.
source: Indeed, we detect 13C-labeled PPIX in parasites grown in 1 µM 5-[13C4]-ALA in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplementary 1), supporting a model that serum ALA stimulates heme biosynthesis during malaria infection in vivo.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 4—figure supplementary 1

claim: ALA, luminol, and DHA have excellent toxicity profiles, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and have each been used clinically.
source: We note that ALA, luminol, and DHA have excellent toxicity profiles, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and have each been used clinically (Bissonnette et al., 2001; Dalton et al., 2002; Gordi and Lepist, 2004; Larkin and Gannicliffe, 2008; Wachowska et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bissonnette et al., 2001; Dalton et al., 2002; Gordi and Lepist, 2004; Larkin and Gannicliffe, 2008; Wachowska et al., 2011

claim: Multidrug-resistant parasites remain susceptible to the photodynamic strategy using ALA, luminol, and enhancers.
source: Multidrug-resistant parasites remain susceptible to this photodynamic strategy, which relies on host enzyme activity outside the genetic control of parasites and thus is refractory to the development of resistance-conferring mutations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing efficacy against Dd2 and Kelch-13 mutant parasites

claim: The photodynamic strategy relying on host enzyme activity is refractory to the development of resistance-conferring mutations.
source: Multidrug-resistant parasites remain susceptible to this photodynamic strategy, which relies on host enzyme activity outside the genetic control of parasites and thus is refractory to the development of resistance-conferring mutations.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of action involving host enzymes

claim: The CL-PDT strategy may be effective against other intraerythrocytic parasites, such as Babesia.
source: This CL-PDT strategy may also be effective against other intraerythrocytic parasites, such as Babesia.
evidence: Speculative extension of the findings

claim: Using artemisinin to stimulate intracellular light emission by luminol for ALA-based PDT may be applicable to treating deep-tissue cancers.
source: Finally, we note that this strategy of using artemisinin to stimulate intracellular light emission by luminol for ALA-based PDT may be applicable to treating deep-tissue cancers, for which poor accessibility to external light also limits current PDT approaches in development for cancer therapy (Celli et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculative extension of the findings, with citation to Celli et al., 2010

claim: Artemisinin has shown promising anti-cancer properties on its own.
source: Artemisinin has shown promising anti-cancer properties on its own (Nakase et al., 2008), and thus its combination with ALA and luminol may provide potent synergy for cancer chemotherapy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakase et al., 2008

claim: The combination of artemisinin with ALA and luminol may provide potent synergy for cancer chemotherapy.
source: Artemisinin has shown promising anti-cancer properties on its own (Nakase et al., 2008), and thus its combination with ALA and luminol may provide potent synergy for cancer chemotherapy.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known properties of artemisinin

claim: Vestigial host enzymes in the cytoplasm of Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes contribute to ALA-stimulated heme biosynthesis.
source: Here we use photodynamic imaging, mass spectrometry, parasite gene disruption, and chemical probes to reveal that vestigial host enzymes in the cytoplasm of Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes contribute to ALA-stimulated heme biosynthesis
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript

claim: ALA uptake depends on parasite-established permeability pathways.
source: and that ALA uptake depends on parasite-established permeability pathways.
evidence: Supported by experiments using TMP-regulated parasites and furosemide

claim: PPIX accumulation in infected erythrocytes can be harnessed for antimalarial chemotherapy using luminol-based chemiluminescence.
source: We show that PPIX accumulation in infected erythrocytes can be harnessed for antimalarial chemotherapy using luminol-based chemiluminescence and combinatorial stimulation by low-dose artemisinin to photoactivate PPIX to produce cytotoxic reactive oxygen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing growth inhibition with ALA, luminol, and artemisinin combinations

claim: This photodynamic strategy has the advantage of exploiting host enzymes refractory to resistance-conferring mutations.
source: This photodynamic strategy has the advantage of exploiting host enzymes refractory to resistance-conferring mutations.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of action and supported by efficacy against drug-resistant parasites

claim: Untreated parasites display only background auto-fluorescence from hemozoin crystals in the parasite digestive vacuole.
source: Untreated parasites imaged on an epifluorescence microscope display only background auto-fluorescence from hemozoin crystals in the parasite digestive vacuole (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B

claim: Exogenous ALA bypasses the regulated step of ALA production by ALA synthase in heme biosynthesis.
source: Production of 5-ALA by ALA synthase (ALAS) is the regulated step in heme biosynthesis. Exogenous ALA bypasses this step and stimulates biosynthetic flux
evidence: Based on established knowledge of heme biosynthesis

claim: Conversion of PPIX to heme by FC becomes rate limiting when exogenous ALA stimulates biosynthetic flux.
source: Exogenous ALA bypasses this step and stimulates biosynthetic flux, leading to accumulation of the final intermediate, PPIX, since conversion of PPIX to heme by FC becomes rate limiting (Kennedy et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kennedy et al., 1990

claim: PPIX is fluorescent.
source: PPIX is fluorescent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Photodynamic imaging has been exploited for visualizing cancerous tumor boundaries during surgical resection.
source: and its cellular accumulation can be directly visualized by fluorescence microscopy using a phenomenon called 'photodynamic imaging' that has been exploited for visualizing cancerous tumor boundaries during surgical resection (Celli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Celli et al., 2010

claim: Hemozoin dynamics serve as an internal biomarker of food vacuole integrity and parasite viability.
source: Although the origin and physiological significance of this motion remain unknown, hemozoin dynamics serve as an internal biomarker of food vacuole integrity and parasite viability (Sigala and Goldberg, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sigala and Goldberg, 2014

claim: The heme biosynthesis pathway in human cells is distributed between mitochondria and the cytoplasm.
source: The heme biosynthesis pathway in human cells is distributed between mitochondria and the cytoplasm, with four cytosolic enzymes that correspond to the four apicoplast-targeted enzymes in Plasmodium parasites (Ponka, 1997, 1999; van Dooren et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ponka, 1997, 1999 and van Dooren et al., 2012

claim: During human erythropoiesis, precursor reticulocytes carry out prolific heme biosynthesis.
source: During human erythropoiesis, precursor reticulocytes carry out prolific heme biosynthesis, but this activity is absent in mature erythrocytes due to loss of mitochondria and their constituent heme biosynthesis enzymes, including ALAS and FC (Ponka, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ponka, 1997

claim: Heme biosynthesis activity is absent in mature erythrocytes due to loss of mitochondria and their constituent heme biosynthesis enzymes, including ALAS and FC.
source: During human erythropoiesis, precursor reticulocytes carry out prolific heme biosynthesis, but this activity is absent in mature erythrocytes due to loss of mitochondria and their constituent heme biosynthesis enzymes, including ALAS and FC (Ponka, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ponka, 1997

claim: A soluble fraction of human CPO persists in the erythrocyte cytoplasm after maturation of precursor reticulocytes and mitochondrial loss.
source: Our observation that disruption of the parasite CPO had no effect on conversion of ALA into heme by intraerythrocytic parasites suggests that a soluble fraction of human CPO, which is thought to be predominantly targeted to the mitochondrial intermembrane space (IMS) (Ponka, 1997; van Dooren et al., 2012), persists in the erythrocyte cytoplasm after maturation of precursor reticulocytes and mitochondrial loss.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations, with citations to Ponka, 1997 and van Dooren et al., 2012

claim: Mitochondrial IMS proteins, such as cytochrome c, are known to partition into the cytoplasm under certain conditions.
source: Indeed, other mitochondrial IMS proteins, such as cytochrome c, are known to partition into the cytoplasm under certain conditions (Liu et al., 1996; Soltys and Gupta, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 1996 and Soltys and Gupta, 2000

claim: CPO catalyzes production of protoporphyrinogen IX, which in the oxygen-rich environment of erythrocytes can spontaneously oxidize to form PPIX.
source: CPO catalyzes production of protoporphyrinogen IX, which in the oxygen-rich environment of erythrocytes can spontaneously oxidize to form PPIX (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2008

claim: Saponin selectively permeabilizes host cell membranes while leaving parasite membranes intact.
source: To dissect these parallel pathways and test whether the parasite pathway alone, in the absence of host enzymes, can support heme biosynthesis from ALA, we fractionated parasite-infected erythrocytes using saponin to selectively permeabilize host cell membranes while leaving parasite membranes intact (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of saponin's properties, referenced in Figure 5A

claim: Parasites treated with saponin remain metabolically active for 5–6 hr or longer.
source: Parasites treated in this fashion remain metabolically active for 5–6 hr or longer, retain a membrane potential, accumulate fluorescent dyes such as MitoTracker Red (Figure 5B,C), and carry out DNA synthesis (Izumo et al., 1987; Cobbold et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C, and citations to Izumo et al., 1987 and Cobbold et al., 2011

claim: The cobA protein catalyzes conversion of uroporphyrinogen III into the red fluorescent products sirohydrochlorin and trimethylpyrrocorphin.
source: The cobA protein catalyzes conversion of the heme biosynthesis intermediate uroporphyrinogen III into the red fluorescent products sirohydrochlorin and trimethylpyrrocorphin (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6A
